people.long_bio: Theodore II reigned for only about twenty days, probably in December 897. He called a synod that restored the clergy degraded by Stephen VI and recognised the orders conferred by Formosus. He also had Formosus's body, which had been thrown into the Tiber, given honourable burial again in St Peter's.

In synods at Rome and Ravenna he condemned the 'cadaver synod' of Stephen VI, forbade re-ordinations and restored deposed clergy. To curb violence at papal elections, he required that a new pope be consecrated only in the presence of imperial envoys. He backed Emperor Lambert and approved a church hierarchy for Moravia.

people.short_bio: A Roman noble who had been passed over in 898 and took the papacy in 904 with the help of the Roman aristocracy. He rebuilt the Lateran Basilica but is remembered for his ties to the powerful family of Theophylact.
people.long_bio: Sergius, son of Benedict, had been a rival candidate in 898 and spent years in exile. Consecrated in January 904 after the Romans overthrew Christopher, he declared the ordinations of Formosus null, reopening old wounds. He restored the Lateran Basilica, which had collapsed, and recognised the fourth marriage of the Byzantine emperor Leo VI. Hostile writers claimed he killed his predecessors and fathered the future John XI with Marozia; the Catholic Encyclopedia judges these charges doubtful. He died in April 911.

He granted the pallium to the archbishop of Reims and to the patriarch of Constantinople, and many privileges to Cluny.

people.short_bio: A Roman priest, probably a monk, who was pope from 936 to 939 under Alberic II. He called Odo of Cluny to Rome and supported monastic reform.
people.long_bio: Leo VII owed his election to Alberic, prince of the Romans. He invited Abbot Odo of Cluny to Rome, where Odo helped make peace between Alberic and King Hugh of Italy. He named Archbishop Frederick of Mainz his vicar in Germany to promote reform; he forbade the forced baptism of Jews but allowed their expulsion from cities. Most of his bulls favour monasteries, especially Cluny. He died in July 939.

people.short_bio: Octavian, son of Alberic II, ruler of Rome, became pope at about eighteen in 955. He crowned Otto I emperor in 962, then plotted against him and was deposed, dying in 964.
people.long_bio: Before his death Alberic II had the Romans swear to elect his son Octavian pope; he was chosen in December 955, aged at most eighteen, and took the name John. Threatened by King Berengar II, he called on Otto I of Germany, whom he crowned emperor on 2 February 962. He soon intrigued against Otto, who returned to Rome; a synod deposed John in December 963 and chose Leo VIII. John came back early in 964, took revenge on his opponents and annulled Leo's election, but died on 14 May 964. Hostile writers, chiefly Liutprand of Cremona, describe his life as scandalous.

people.long_bio: Leo, the 'protonotary', was a layman when a synod under Otto I deposed John XII and elected him in December 963; he received all the orders within days. When Otto left, the Romans expelled him; after John's death they chose Benedict V. Otto returned in the summer of 964, and Leo had Benedict deposed. He died early in 965. The Vatican list counts him as pope from 963, though the Catholic Encyclopedia considers him a true pope only from 964, after Benedict V was deposed.

people.long_bio: On the death of John XII in May 964 the Romans elected Benedict, a cardinal-deacon known for his learning, rather than accept Leo VIII. He died at Hamburg on 4 July 965; his remains were later brought back to Rome.

people.short_bio: A Roman bishop of Narni, elected with Otto I's support in 965. Briefly imprisoned by Roman nobles, he returned with imperial help and crowned Otto II co-emperor.
people.long_bio: John was from a Roman noble family and had been bishop of Narni. Elected in 965, he was seized by hostile nobles that December and held in Castel Sant'Angelo and the Campagna, but escaped to Capua and returned in November 966 when Otto I's army approached. He crowned Otto II co-emperor on Christmas Day 967 and blessed his marriage to the Byzantine princess Theophano in 972. He raised Magdeburg, Capua and Benevento to archbishoprics and favoured Cluny. He died on 6 September 972.

He opposed the French bishops who deposed Archbishop Arnulf of Reims and replaced him with Gerbert, the future Sylvester II. On 31 January 993 he solemnly canonized Bishop Ulrich of Augsburg. people.short_bio: Bruno, a young German noble and cousin of Emperor Otto III, became the first German pope in 996. He crowned Otto emperor, was driven out by Crescentius and an antipope, and was restored by Otto shortly before his death in 999.
people.long_bio: Bruno was a chaplain at Otto III's court when the emperor chose him as pope; consecrated in May 996, aged about 26, he took the name Gregory and crowned Otto emperor on 21 May. When Otto left Italy, the patrician Crescentius drove Gregory out and set up the antipope John XVI. Gregory excommunicated them, and Otto's return in 998 ended the revolt. He pressed King Robert II of France over his marriage to Bertha and treated Gerbert's claim to Reims as unlawful. He died early in 999 and was buried in St Peter's.
actions: Crowned Otto III emperor (996)
Excommunicated Crescentius and the antipope John XVI
Pressed King Robert II of France over an unlawful marriage
people.context: The young emperor Otto III dreamed of renewing the Roman Empire with Rome as its capital and the pope as his partner. The Crescentii resisted him; new Christian kingdoms in Poland and Hungary were taking shape.

people.short_bio: Gerbert of Aurillac, a scholar of humble birth famed for his learning in mathematics and astronomy, became the first French pope in 999. He worked closely with Otto III and set up the churches of Poland and Hungary.
people.long_bio: Gerbert grew up as an oblate at the abbey of Aurillac and studied the sciences in Catalonia, at Vich and Ripoll. He became a celebrated teacher at Reims, abbot of Bobbio, contested archbishop of Reims and then archbishop of Ravenna. Chosen pope with Otto III's support in 999, he took the name Sylvester. He created the archbishoprics of Gniezno in Poland and Esztergom in Hungary and recognised Stephen of Hungary as king. He opposed simony and clerical concubinage, and died in Rome on 12 May 1003.

people.short_bio: Sicco, a Roman who had been married before ordination, was raised to the papacy in 1003 by John Crescentius. He died after less than six months.
people.long_bio: John XVII was consecrated in June 1003, owing his elevation to John Crescentius, who controlled Rome. Nothing is recorded of his acts. He died on 6 November 1003.
people.context: Rome was dominated by the Crescentii family, while the German emperors claimed a say in papal elections. Byzantium still held southern Italy, and the Saracens raided its coasts. Monastic reform spread from Cluny across western Europe.

people.short_bio: Phasianus, son of a Roman priest, was pope from 1003 to 1009 under the influence of the Crescentii. He approved the new diocese of Bamberg founded by King Henry II.
people.long_bio: John XVIII was consecrated at Christmas 1003. At a Roman synod in 1007 he approved the founding of the see of Bamberg by Henry II of Germany. He sent the pallium to the archbishops of Trier and Canterbury and defended the privileges of the abbey of Fleury. According to one catalogue of popes he died as a monk at St Paul's outside the Walls, in 1009.

people.short_bio: Peter, a shoemaker's son from the Pigna district of Rome and bishop of Albano, was pope from 1009 to 1012. He worked to loosen the grip of the Crescentii and was known as a friend of the poor.
people.long_bio: Nicknamed 'Bucca Porci', 'pig's snout', Peter had been bishop of Albano from 1004. As pope he strengthened the pro-German party against the patrician John Crescentius, exempted several monasteries from episcopal control, and helped the poor during a famine. He died on 12 May 1012 and was buried in the Lateran.

people.short_bio: Theophylact, son of Count Gregory of Tusculum, took the papacy by force in 1012, probably still a layman, and proved an able ruler. He crowned Henry II emperor, fought the Saracens and backed church reform.
people.long_bio: Benedict VIII was imposed on Rome by his family in May 1012 and drove out a rival candidate. He broke the power of the Crescentii, crowned Henry II emperor on 14 February 1014, and at Henry's request agreed that the Creed be sung at Mass in Rome. He joined the war against the Saracens of Mujahid, who were defeated in 1016, and supported the Normans in the south. With Henry he held a synod at Pavia in 1022 against clerical marriage and simony, and he visited Bamberg in 1020. He died on 9 April 1024.

people.short_bio: Romanus, brother of Benedict VIII, was a layman ruling Rome as consul when he succeeded his brother in 1024. He crowned Conrad II emperor and invited Guido of Arezzo to explain his new musical notation.
people.long_bio: Romanus received all the holy orders in quick succession after his election in 1024. Under pressure from Roman opinion he refused the Byzantine request to recognise the patriarch of Constantinople as 'ecumenical'. He crowned Conrad II emperor on 26 March 1027, took Cluny under his protection, and brought Guido of Arezzo to Rome to show his system of musical notation. He died in 1032.

people.short_bio: Theophylact of Tusculum, nephew of the two previous popes, was made pope in 1032 and is the only man to have held the office three times. Driven out in 1044, he returned in 1045, gave up the see for money, and seized it again in 1047-1048.
people.long_bio: Benedict IX was elected in 1032 through his family's power; chroniclers made him a boy, but Treccani thinks he was about twenty-five. His conduct provoked a revolt in 1044, and Sylvester III was set up in his place, but Benedict returned in March 1045. On 1 May 1045 he resigned in favour of his godfather John Gratian, Gregory VI, in return for a large sum. The synod of Sutri in 1046 set all three claimants aside. After the death of Clement II he seized Rome again from late 1047 until mid-1048, when Damasus II was installed. He was still alive in 1055 and probably died around the end of that year; a tradition says he died in penance at Grottaferrata.
actions: Held the papacy three times (1032-1044, 1045, 1047-1048)
Resigned the office to Gregory VI for money (1045)
Was set aside by the synod of Sutri (1046)
people.context: In the 1040s Rome had three rival claimants at once, and the papacy was openly bought and sold. In 1046 the German king Henry III came to Italy, had the synod of Sutri remove the rival popes, and installed a series of German bishops, opening the way for the great church reform of the eleventh century.
people.public_uncertainty: His age at election and the scandals told of him are disputed; the date and place of his death are uncertain.
open_questions: Roster end of third tenure '... VIII.1048' vs Vatican Italian table '... VII.1048'.
CE says he was driven out in November 1048; Damasus II was consecrated 17 July 1048.

people.short_bio: John, bishop of Sabina, was elected pope in January 1045 after Benedict IX was driven from Rome. Within weeks Benedict expelled him, and the synod of Sutri deposed him in 1046; he went back to his diocese.
people.long_bio: Sylvester III was chosen by a Roman faction, probably the Crescentii, after a revolt against Benedict IX. Benedict excommunicated him and drove him out in March 1045, and he returned to his see in the Sabina. At Sutri in December 1046 he was condemned for occupying the Apostolic See. He continued to act as bishop of Sabina and appears in records until 1062; he had probably died by 1063. The Vatican list counts him as a pope, though he is often called an antipope.

people.short_bio: John Gratian, archpriest of San Giovanni a Porta Latina, paid Benedict IX to give up the papacy in 1045, hoping to rescue the office. The synod of Sutri judged the bargain simoniacal, and he stepped down in 1046.
people.long_bio: Gregory VI was respected for his piety and may have belonged to the reform party. He paid a large sum to his spiritual kinsman Benedict IX, who resigned on 1 May 1045. At the synod of Sutri in December 1046 the bishops found his election tainted by simony, and he laid down the office. Henry III took him to Germany in 1047, with the young Hildebrand, later Gregory VII, as his chaplain. He died there, probably at Cologne, around the end of 1047 or early 1048.

people.short_bio: Suidger, a Saxon noble and bishop of Bamberg, was chosen pope by Henry III at the synod of Sutri and enthroned on Christmas Day 1046. He crowned Henry emperor, condemned simony, and died within a year; he is buried in Bamberg Cathedral.
people.long_bio: Suidger had been a canon of Halberstadt and chaplain to Henry III, who made him bishop of Bamberg. Enthroned in St Peter's on 25 December 1046, he crowned Henry and Agnes of Poitou emperor and empress the same day. A Roman synod in January 1047 punished simony with excommunication. He died near Pesaro on 9 October 1047; rumours of poison were circulated, and a 1942 examination of his remains found signs of lead poisoning, though Treccani thinks malaria more likely. He is the only pope buried in Germany.

people.short_bio: Poppo, bishop of Brixen in the Tyrol, was named pope by Henry III and enthroned in July 1048. He died at Palestrina after only about twenty-three days, probably of malaria.
people.long_bio: Poppo was a trusted ally of Henry III and had been bishop of Brixen since about 1040. Named by the emperor in late 1047, he could enter Rome only in July 1048, after Benedict IX was driven out with the help of Boniface of Canossa. He was enthroned on 17 July 1048 but died at Palestrina on 9 August, where he had gone to escape the summer heat. He was buried at San Lorenzo fuori le Mura.

birthplace.label: Eguisheim
birthplace.note: Vatican: 'Alsaziano'. CE: born 21 June 1002 at Egisheim near Colmar, Alsace; Wikipedia agrees. Then in the Duchy of Swabia, Holy Roman Empire.

saint.note: Vatican Italian table marks 'S.'. Vatican News saint-of-the-day lists St Leo IX, Pope, on 19 April (feast verified). CE: worker of miracles, entered in the Roman Martyrology; no canonization date given. Wikipedia: canonized 1082 by Gregory VII (unsourced there; an elevation of relics). Classified pre_congregation; the 1082 date is supplementary and should be treated as provisional.

people.short_bio: Bruno of Egisheim, an Alsatian noble and for over twenty years bishop of Toul, became pope in 1049 and launched the great eleventh-century reform of the Church. He travelled widely holding councils against simony, but was captured by the Normans in 1053 and died in 1054.
people.long_bio: A cousin of Emperor Conrad II, Bruno was bishop of Toul from 1027. Nominated by Henry III, he insisted on election by the clergy and people of Rome, which he entered as a barefoot pilgrim, and was enthroned on 12 February 1049. He gathered reformers such as Hildebrand and Humbert, and held synods at Rome, Pavia, Reims, Mainz and elsewhere against simony and clerical marriage, earning the name 'the apostolic pilgrim'. He condemned the teaching of Berengar of Tours on the Eucharist. In 1053 his army was defeated by the Normans at Civitate and he was held at Benevento. He died in Rome on 19 April 1054; soon after, his legates excommunicated Patriarch Michael Cerularius, a milestone in the split between East and West.
actions: Led councils across Europe against simony and clerical marriage
Condemned Berengar of Tours
Was defeated and captured by the Normans at Civitate (1053)
Sent the legates whose mission ended in the 1054 break with Constantinople
people.context: Church reform, long nurtured in monasteries like Cluny and Gorze, now reached the papacy itself with the support of Emperor Henry III. The Normans were carving out lordships in southern Italy, and relations with Constantinople were strained over rites and papal authority, leading to the mutual excommunications of 1054.
open_questions: Exact form of the 1082 recognition (elevation of relics by Gregory VII) not verified in a Vatican or CE source.

notes: Rows 115-152 complete (36 people; Benedict IX = rows 145,147,150 as one record). Feast days: only Leo IX (19 April, Vatican News). Only saint in range: Leo IX (Vatican 'S.'); all others none. Birth-field issues: John XII roster 'Counts of Tusculum' is a family label (son of Alberic II; birthplace undocumented, set region Rome). Benedict VIII, John XIX, Benedict IX have blank roster birth: set region Rome/Tusculum (25 km) with public note. Conflicts with Vatican birth field: Gregory V 'Saxony' (family of Worms/Carinthia; set region Worms, alternative Saxony in note); Sylvester III and Gregory VI 'Rome' kept but Treccani says origin unknown (public notes); Sylvester II 'Aquitaine' set region near Aurillac; Leo V Ardea set region (born at unlocated Priapi near Ardea); John X Tossignano is 'probably' per Treccani. Roster/Italian table date discrepancy: Benedict IX row 150 end VIII.1048 (roster) vs VII.1048 (Italian table). Agapetus II: CE death Aug 956 vs roster XII.955. Leo VIII/Benedict V overlap in 964 noted in both records. CE numbering differs for Stephen VII/VIII and John XV/XVIII (alt_names note older numbering).
